results.name: single_example_multiple_targets_rate
results.description: Yes rate on one-example sets (example > 1) for non-example targets that are multiples of the example (10->80, 11->55, 6->18); observed above null means the model still under-generalizes a lone example to its multiples rule (below = over-generalizes).
results.code:
# name: single_example_multiple_targets_rate
# description: Yes rate on one-example sets (example > 1) for non-example targets that are multiples of the example (10->80, 11->55, 6->18); observed above null means the model still under-generalizes a lone example to its multiples rule (below = over-generalizes).
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    d = df[n == 1]
    x = d["number_set"].astype(int)
    t = d["target"].astype(int)
    m = (x > 1) & (t != x) & (t % x == 0)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(d.loc[m, "rating"].mean())

results.name: in_minus_out_range_3plus
results.description: For sets with 3+ examples, non-example-target yes rate inside [min,max] of the examples minus outside it; observed above null means people confine generalization to the examples' range more than the model (below = the model over-confines, e.g. via its range-size prior).
results.code:
# name: in_minus_out_range_3plus
# description: For sets with 3+ examples, non-example-target yes rate inside [min,max] of the examples minus outside it; observed above null means people confine generalization to the examples' range more than the model (below = the model over-confines, e.g. via its range-size prior).
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    d = df[n >= 3]
    sets = d["number_set"].unique()
    lo = {}; hi = {}; exs = {}
    for s in sets:
        xs = [int(v) for v in str(s).split(",")]
        lo[s] = min(xs); hi[s] = max(xs); exs[s] = set(xs)
    t = d["target"].astype(int)
    a = d["number_set"].map(lo); b = d["number_set"].map(hi)
    isex = pd.Series([tt in exs[s] for s, tt in zip(d["number_set"].values, t.values)], index=d.index)
    inside = (t >= a) & (t <= b) & ~isex
    outside = ((t < a) | (t > b))
    if inside.sum() == 0 or outside.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(d.loc[inside, "rating"].mean() - d.loc[outside, "rating"].mean())

results.name: single_example_nonmultiple_targets_rate
results.description: Yes rate on one-example sets for non-example targets that are NOT multiples of the example (6->8, 14->74, 100->20, 1->27 count as non-multiples except x=1); observed above null means people generalize a lone example more diffusely than the model (below = model too diffuse beyond the multiples rule).
results.code:
# name: single_example_nonmultiple_targets_rate
# description: Yes rate on one-example sets for non-example targets that are NOT multiples of the example (6->8, 14->74, 100->20, 1->27 count as non-multiples except x=1); observed above null means people generalize a lone example more diffusely than the model (below = model too diffuse beyond the multiples rule).
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    d = df[n == 1]
    x = d["number_set"].astype(int)
    t = d["target"].astype(int)
    m = (t != x) & ~((x > 1) & (t % x == 0))
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(d.loc[m, "rating"].mean())

results.name: within_set_target_sd
results.description: Mean over sets with >=5 distinct targets of the SD of per-target yes rates within the set; observed above null means people discriminate between targets of the same set more sharply than the model (below = model's gradients are too sharp / all-or-none).
results.code:
# name: within_set_target_sd
# description: Mean over sets with >=5 distinct targets of the SD of per-target yes rates within the set; observed above null means people discriminate between targets of the same set more sharply than the model (below = model's gradients are too sharp / all-or-none).
def test_statistic(df):
    c = df.groupby(["number_set", "target"])["rating"].mean().reset_index()
    g = c.groupby("number_set")["rating"]
    sd = g.std(ddof=0)[g.size() >= 5]
    return float(sd.mean()) if len(sd) else 0.0

results.name: two_example_generalization_rate
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets on sets with exactly two examples; observed above null means the model's size principle/range prior is too strict with two examples (below = too lenient).
results.code:
# name: two_example_generalization_rate
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets on sets with exactly two examples; observed above null means the model's size principle/range prior is too strict with two examples (below = too lenient).
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    d = df[n == 2]
    ex = d["number_set"].str.split(",")
    t = d["target"].astype(int)
    a = ex.str[0].astype(int); b = ex.str[1].astype(int)
    m = (t != a) & (t != b)
    return float(d.loc[m, "rating"].mean()) if m.sum() else 0.0

results.name: shared_last_digit_nonmatching_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets whose last digit differs from the common last digit of 3+-example sets whose examples all share one last digit (72,92,82,42 -> 25); observed below null means people reject non-matching numbers (even inside the range) more sharply than the model, whose broad-range prior lets intervals leak (above = less sharply).

results.name: four_minus_three_example_rate
results.description: Non-example-target yes rate on four-example sets minus that on three-example sets (observed ~+0.10); observed above null means people do not narrow generalization from 3 to 4 examples as the model's accumulating size principle predicts (below = they narrow more).
results.code:
# name: four_minus_three_example_rate
# description: Non-example-target yes rate on four-example sets minus that on three-example sets (observed ~+0.10); observed above null means people do not narrow generalization from 3 to 4 examples as the model's accumulating size principle predicts (below = they narrow more).
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1
    tstr = "," + df["target"].astype(str) + ","
    sets = "," + df["number_set"].str.replace(" ", "") + ","
    is_example = pd.Series([a in b for a, b in zip(tstr.values, sets.values)], index=df.index)
    r4 = df.loc[(n == 4) & ~is_example, "rating"].mean()
    r3 = df.loc[(n == 3) & ~is_example, "rating"].mean()
    v = r4 - r3
    return float(v) if np.isfinite(v) else 0.0

results.name: common_multiple_contrast
results.description: For 2+-example sets whose examples share a common divisor k in 3..12 (largest such k), mean over sets of (yes rate on non-example multiples of k) minus (yes rate on non-multiples); observed below null means people use arithmetic "multiples of k" rules less sharply than the model (above = more sharply).
results.code:
# name: common_multiple_contrast
# description: For 2+-example sets whose examples share a common divisor k in 3..12 (largest such k), mean over sets of (yes rate on non-example multiples of k) minus (yes rate on non-multiples); observed below null means people use arithmetic "multiples of k" rules less sharply than the model (above = more sharply).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].unique()
    kmap = {}; exs = {}
    for s in sets:
        xs = [int(v) for v in str(s).split(",")]
        if len(xs) < 2:
            continue
        ks = [k for k in range(3, 13) if all(v % k == 0 for v in xs)]
        if ks:
            kmap[s] = max(ks); exs[s] = set(xs)
    d = df[df["number_set"].isin(list(kmap))]
    if len(d) == 0:
        return 0.0
    t = d["target"].astype(int).values
    sv = d["number_set"].values
    notex = np.array([tt not in exs[s] for s, tt in zip(sv, t)])
    k = d["number_set"].map(kmap).values
    mult = (t % k) == 0
    tmp = pd.DataFrame({"s": sv, "m": mult, "r": d["rating"].values})[notex]
    agg = tmp.groupby(["s", "m"])["r"].mean().unstack()
    if True not in agg.columns or False not in agg.columns:
        return 0.0
    diff = (agg[True] - agg[False]).dropna()
    return float(diff.mean()) if len(diff) else 0.0
